list_all_my_buckets/allowed_on_every_buc.note: AWS's own example says an Allow on arn:aws:s3:::* lets a user list all buckets, but the simulator denies: it matched the patterns against the * it was sent (EvalResourceName *), which says nothing about the resource a real request carries. The analyzer follows the example: it matches the request as arn:aws:s3:::, a bucket ARN with an empty name.
list_all_my_buckets/allowed_on_every_buc.quote: The AllowS3ListRead statement in this policy allows Carlos to view a list of all of the buckets in the account.

not_principal/names_the_account_and_anot.note: EXPLICIT_DENY: naming the account didn't exclude everyone in it. Weak evidence, since the simulator also denies the user the policy names (names_the_account_and_the_caller).

not_principal/names_the_account_and_the_.note: NotPrincipal names both the account and kwong, as AWS recommends, yet the simulator still denies kwong. Every NotPrincipal case came back EXPLICIT_DENY, so its NotPrincipal answers are weak evidence.
not_principal/names_the_account_and_the_.quote: The NotPrincipal element uses "Effect":"Deny" to deny access to all principals except the principal specified in the NotPrincipal element.

not_principal/names_the_caller.note: EXPLICIT_DENY: consistent with AWS checking the account first. Weak evidence, since the simulator also denies kwong when the account is named too (names_the_account_and_the_caller).

role_principal_case/role_name_in_lowerca.note: Case matters in the simulator: role/district/campusapp doesn't name the CampusApp role. AWS documents that a saved trust policy turns a role ARN into the role's unique ID, which the simulator can't do for an example role.

scenarios/bucket_policy_role_grant_is_li.note: The simulator allows a bucket policy grant to the caller's role although the role's boundary doesn't allow the read (AllowedByPermissionsBoundary false).
scenarios/bucket_policy_role_grant_is_li.quote: Resource-based policies that grant permissions to an IAM role ARN are limited by an implicit deny in a permissions boundary or session policy.

scenarios/incomplete_arn_allow_is_comple.note: The simulator doesn't complete arn:aws:sqs, so the Allow covers no queue: the exact case AWS gives as an example.
scenarios/incomplete_arn_allow_is_comple.quote: When you specify an incomplete ARN (one with fewer than the standard six fields) in an identity-based policy, AWS automatically completes the ARN by adding wildcard characters (*) to all missing fields. For example, specifying arn:aws:sqs is equivalent to arn:aws:sqs:*:*:*

scenarios/incomplete_arn_is_completed_wi.note: The simulator doesn't complete arn:aws:s3, so the Deny misses.
scenarios/incomplete_arn_is_completed_wi.quote: When you specify an incomplete ARN (one with fewer than the standard six fields) in an identity-based policy, AWS automatically completes the ARN by adding wildcard characters (*) to all missing fields. For example, specifying arn:aws:sqs is equivalent to arn:aws:sqs:*:*:*

scenarios/scp_skips_service_linked_role.note: The simulator applies the SCPs to a service-linked role caller (AllowedByOrganizations false).
scenarios/scp_skips_service_linked_role.quote: SCPs do not affect any service-linked role. Service-linked roles enable other AWS services to integrate with AWS Organizations and can't be restricted by SCPs.

scp_short_arn/short_arn_in_an_scp_deny.note: The simulator doesn't complete arn:aws:s3 in an SCP Deny, so it allows the read. AWS documents completion only for identity-based policies, and the simulator skips it there too (the two incomplete_arn scenarios), so this is weak evidence. The analyzer refuses a short ARN in an SCP.

short_arns_in_arn_operators/four_fields_.note: AWS rejects the simulation (InvalidInput). GetContextKeysForCustomPolicy accepted the policy.

short_arns_in_arn_operators/three_fields.note: AWS rejects the simulation (InvalidInput). GetContextKeysForCustomPolicy accepted the policy.

star_grant_and_boundary/account_principa.note: The simulator allows the read although the boundary doesn't. account_principal_without_identity_allow shows why: it treats naming the account as a grant to everyone in it, with or without an identity policy.
star_grant_and_boundary/account_principa.quote: You can specify AWS account identifiers in the Principal element of a resource-based policy or in condition keys that support principals. This delegates authority to the account.

star_grant_and_boundary/account_principa.note: With no identity policy that allows the read, and a boundary that doesn't, the simulator still allows it: naming the account grants the read by itself.
star_grant_and_boundary/account_principa.quote: You can specify AWS account identifiers in the Principal element of a resource-based policy or in condition keys that support principals. This delegates authority to the account.

wildcards_and_colons/short_pattern_star_.note: The simulator doesn't complete arn:aws:sqs:us-*-alerts, and its * then runs from the region field through the account field. Completed as AWS documents, the pattern matches no queue.
wildcards_and_colons/short_pattern_star_.quote: When you specify an incomplete ARN (one with fewer than the standard six fields) in an identity-based policy, AWS automatically completes the ARN by adding wildcard characters (*) to all missing fields. For example, specifying arn:aws:sqs is equivalent to arn:aws:sqs:*:*:*
